matter_reference_date_basis: matter_reference_date recorded in candidates/matters/M100.json, taken from the OCTOBER 2018 exam session. Every temporal check below is made against October 2018, which is before the Notaries (Amendment) Acts No. 31 of 2022 and No. 6 of 2024 and the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, all of which are carried by the consolidated corpus text.
corpus_gaps: Rule (10) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance was in force in October 2018 and was repealed only by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(4). The consolidated corpus text of section 31 jumps from rule (9) to rule (11) and the repealing section does not reproduce what it repealed, so the content of a rule that sat among the witness and identification rules at the matter date cannot be read from the corpus. This is the largest single risk to the completeness of the answer.

The corpus text of section 4 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance is the text substituted by Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3, which is after the matter date. Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(2) repealed the words from 'in the manner hereinafter mentioned;' to the end of the old section without setting them out, so the October 2018 wording of the basic will-execution requirement, including whether the notary and the witnesses had to attest and subscribe in the presence of the testator and of one another, is not recoverable from the corpus.

The corpus text of rule (14) of section 31 is the rule as substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7); the pre-2022 wording of the duty to ascertain the full names of the witnesses before anyone signs is not preserved anywhere in the corpus.

The corpus contains no provision on the competency of a witness as such: no minimum age, no rule about a blind, deaf or illiterate witness, and no rule about a witness related to the testator otherwise than by taking a benefit. Section 10 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance assumes a law of competency without stating it. Those questions belong to the general law and to judicial authority, neither of which is in the corpus.

The Wills Ordinance No. 21 of 1844 as held in the corpus has no section on attesting witnesses at all (its sections run 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9), so nothing in it adds to or qualifies the witness rules relied on here.

No provision in the corpus deals specially with the execution of a will by a testator who is ill or in hospital, apart from rule (36)(c) of section 31, which excuses a non-attorney notary's attendance at his office where the person whose signature is to be taken is believed to be on the point of death. Nothing in the corpus alters the witness requirements for a bedside execution.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: It is and shall be the duty of every notary strictly to observe and act in conformity with the following rules
provisions.why_relevant: Makes each numbered rule in section 31 a mandatory duty of the notary rather than a matter of good practice, so every witness rule relied on below is owed by this notary when he attests the will at the hospital.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 has been in force since 1907. The corpus edition is consolidated to 2024 and prints the text as altered by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024. No amendment event is recorded for the chapeau by any of those Acts, so these words also stood at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
provisions.why_relevant: The first precaution about witnesses: there must be at least two of them and each must subscribe his signature in letters rather than make a mark. It fixes both the minimum number of witnesses and the form of their subscription.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Neither Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 nor Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3 touches rule (8), so this text stood unchanged at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and the witnesses shall sign a declaration at the foot of the deed or instrument that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence.
provisions.why_relevant: The central witness-vetting rule: before he accepts anyone as a witness the notary must satisfy himself that the person is of good repute and well acquainted with the executant and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and he must obtain the witnesses' signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
provisions.temporal_note: The words quoted are unaltered, but their opening context differed at the matter date. In October 2018 rule (9) began 'He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;' (those words were replaced by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6), recorded at PROV-M100-017) and the quoted duty was introduced by the words 'and in the latter case,' (deleted by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), recorded at PROV-M100-018). At the matter date the quoted duty therefore attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant rather than on his own.
provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim and the temporal reconstruction is right, but the role needs a correction: because Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) shows that in October 2018 the vetting and declaration duty was introduced by the words "and in the latter case", that duty attached in terms to the case where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator himself, so on these facts the rule (9) duty is a prudent precaution rather than one the corpus shows to be owed.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
provisions.why_relevant: Governs the manner of signing: the testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in front of all of them. This is the precaution that requires nobody to leave the bedside until every signature is on the will.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (12) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the rule stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another
provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary to state in his attestation the very fact that rule (12) obliges him to secure, so the precaution taken at the bedside must also appear on the face of the will.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7) alter paragraphs (b), (e) and (g) of rule (20) and add paragraph (h); paragraph (a) is untouched and stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: the day, month, and year on which and the place where the said deed or instrument was executed or acknowledged, and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences
provisions.why_relevant: Requires the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses, and the place of execution, to appear in the attestation. Here the place is a hospital ward, so the notary must know and record where each witness lives.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (c) of rule (20) is not among the paragraphs amended by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11) or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(7); it stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: such devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition, or appointment shall, so far only as concerns such person attesting the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or the wife or husband of such person, or any person claiming under such person or wife or husband, be utterly null and void
provisions.why_relevant: The disqualification that matters most in choosing witnesses to a will: a beneficiary, or the spouse of a beneficiary, who attests the will loses the gift. The notary's precaution is to ensure that neither witness, nor either witness's spouse, takes anything under the will.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 11 has been in force since 1840. No amendment event is recorded for it in the corpus, and neither Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 nor Act No. 4 of 2024 touches it, so this is also the October 2018 text.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any case in which the person executing or acknowledging the same shall be or profess to be unable to read the same, or in which such person shall require him to read over the same, unless and until he shall have read over and explained the same, or caused the same to be explained, in the presence and hearing of such person and, except in the case of wills and codicils, in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
provisions.why_relevant: Qualifies what the witnesses must be present for. Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but wills and codicils are expressly excepted from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (11) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; it stood in this form at October 2018. Section 34(1)(b) treats a breach of rule (11) as an offence.
provisions.verifier_note: Rule (11) itself is verified verbatim and was unamended at the matter date, but the temporal note's reference to section 34(1)(b) reads the post-2022 penalty section: section 34 was substituted in its entirety by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so the corpus does not show how a breach of rule (11) was punished in October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: whether the same was read over by the person executing the same, or read and explained by him, the said notary, to the said person in the presence of the attesting witnesses
provisions.why_relevant: The attestation must record whether the will was read over by the testator himself or read and explained to him in the presence of the attesting witnesses, so the notary must settle which course was followed and then state it.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. Paragraph (d) of rule (20) is untouched by the 2022 and 2024 amendments and stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument
provisions.why_relevant: The witnesses' task does not end with the original: the same two witnesses must also sign the protocol copy the notary keeps, so the notary must have the protocol ready at the bedside before they disperse.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (24) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time when such deed was executed or acknowledged
provisions.why_relevant: Attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is a criminal offence, not merely a breach of a rule. It is the sanction that makes the presence requirement in rule (12) a real precaution.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 39 has been in force since 1907. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.19(1) altered other words of paragraph (c) ('signature or mark' became 'signature, and the left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, as the case may be') and s.19(2) raised the penalty; the words quoted here fall outside both substitutions and stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
provisions.why_relevant: Keeps the notary himself out of the instrument. He cannot make up the number by acting as one of the two witnesses to a will he attests, and cannot attest a will in which he takes an interest.
provisions.temporal_note: Part of section 31, in force since 1907. No amendment event is recorded for rule (13) in Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3; in force in this form at October 2018.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: If any person who shall attest the execution of any will, testament, or codicil shall at the time of the execution thereof, or at any time afterwards, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution thereof, such will, testament, or codicil shall not on that account be invalid.
provisions.why_relevant: Limits the consequence of a bad choice of witness: incompetency of an attesting witness does not by itself invalidate the will. It shows that the sanction for a poorly chosen witness lies elsewhere, chiefly in section 11.
provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: before a notary public and two witnesses who shall be present at the same time
provisions.why_relevant: Sets the number of witnesses and the requirement that they be present at the same time as the notary when the testator signs. It is the source of the two-witness requirement that the notarial rules then work out in detail.
provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text of section 4 is the text as renumbered and substituted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3, which is after the October 2018 matter date, so the wording quoted is not the wording in force at the matter date. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text: Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(2) repeals the words from 'in the manner hereinafter mentioned;' to the end of the section without reproducing them. The requirement of a notary and two witnesses present at the same time is common to the corpus text and to the surviving description of the older text, but for this reason the provision is treated as supporting and not as indispensable.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: No obliteration, interlineations, or other alteration made in any will, testament, or codicil after the execution thereof shall be valid or have any effect, except so far as the words or effect of the will, testament, or codicil before such alteration shall not be apparent, unless such alteration shall be executed in like manner as herein before is required for the execution of the will
provisions.why_relevant: Extends the witness requirement to any alteration made after execution: an alteration has no effect unless executed in the same manner as the will itself, which means before the same class of witnesses.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 7 has been in force since 1840. Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.4 substituted words later in the section ('signature of the testator or testatrix') and added a proviso, both after the matter date; the words quoted here fall outside both changes and stood in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall, before any executant or witness signs or makes a mark and before any executant affixes his left or right thumb impression or any other finger impression or toe impression, ascertain the full names of the executant and witnesses to such deed or instrument
provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary to ascertain the full names of the witnesses before anyone signs, and to describe a witness by both names where the name signed differs from the name in his identification documents.
provisions.temporal_note: Rule (14) as printed in the corpus is the rule substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7), which is after the matter date, so this wording was not in force in October 2018 and the provision is treated as supporting only. The corpus does not carry the pre-2022 text, because s.16(7) substitutes the rule without reproducing what it replaced.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words, "He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto;"
provisions.why_relevant: Recovers the opening words of rule (9) as they stood before 2022, and therefore as they stood at the matter date: the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him. This is the wording against which the facts of this matter, where the notary knows the testator, have to be tested.
provisions.temporal_note: Act No. 31 of 2022 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law here. It is recorded because the words it repeals are the words that were in force at the matter date, and the corpus preserves them only in this amending section.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: in rule (9) thereof, by the substitution for the words "and in the latter case, he shall", of the words, "he shall"; (4) by the repeal of rule (10) thereof;
provisions.why_relevant: Shows two things about the October 2018 text of section 31. First, the witness-vetting duty in rule (9) was then introduced by the words 'and in the latter case, he shall', so it attached in terms to the case where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant. Second, a rule (10) existed at the matter date and was repealed only in 2024, so the consolidated text used here is missing a rule that was in force when this will would have been executed.
provisions.temporal_note: Act No. 6 of 2024 is later than the October 2018 matter date and is not applied as operative law. It is recorded because it identifies wording and a whole rule that were in force at the matter date but are absent from the consolidated corpus text of section 31.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: such creditor, notwithstanding such charge, shall be admitted a witness to prove the execution of such will, testament, or codicil, or to prove the validity or invalidity thereof.
provisions.why_relevant: Background on who may safely be used as a witness: a creditor whose debt is charged on the property by the will is not disqualified from attesting it.
provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
provisions.relevant_excerpt: No person shall, on account of his or her being an executor or executrix of a will, testament, or codicil, be incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove the execution of such will, testament, or codicil
provisions.why_relevant: Background on who may safely be used as a witness: an executor named in the will is not incompetent to attest it and does not forfeit his commission by doing so.
provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1840; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so this is also the October 2018 text.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: No instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form
provisions.why_relevant: Background on consequences: a failure in a matter of form under section 31 does not of itself invalidate the instrument, but the proviso preserves invalidity arising under any other written law, which is where the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance bites.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 33 has been in force since 1907 and no amendment event is recorded for it in the corpus; in force in this form at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: whether the executants of the said deed or instrument are known to him or whether he has identified them by the inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence or whether the witnesses thereto are known to him and in the latter case he shall specify which of the executants or the person acknowledging are known to the said witness
provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Paragraph (b) of rule (20) is the attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses: the notary must state whether he knows the executants himself or whether the witnesses know them, and in the latter case which executant each witness knows. It is the counterpart in the attestation of the identification limb of rule (9), and the researcher's map records paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) of rule (20) but not (b).
provisions.temporal_note: The text quoted is paragraph (b) as substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a), which is after the October 2018 matter date, so this wording was not then in force. Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) repeals the old paragraph (b) without reproducing it, so the October 2018 wording of the one attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses' knowledge of the executant is not recoverable from the corpus. Recorded as a supporting provision and as a corpus gap.
provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31. Added because the map covered rule (20)(a), (c) and (d) but not the witness-facing paragraph (b); it is recorded as inapplicable at the matter date because only the post-2022 wording survives in the corpus.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The precautions a notary must take about witnesses to a last will are laid down expressly by statute: rules (8), (9), (11), (12), (13), (20) and (24) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, reinforced by section 39 of that Ordinance, together with sections 7, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. A complete answer to a three-mark question asking what precautions to take can be given from those provisions without judicial authority or Roman-Dutch common law. Case law would be needed only for the different question whether a particular defect avoids the will, which is not what is asked.

legal_issues.issue: How many witnesses must attest the will and in what form must they subscribe it.
Whom the notary may accept as a witness: what he must satisfy himself about before accepting a person, and who is disqualified by taking a benefit under the will.
In whose presence the testator, the witnesses and the notary must sign, and whether the witnesses must be present when the will is read over.

What the notary must obtain from the witnesses and record about them: the declaration at the foot of the will, their signatures on the protocol, and their full names and residences in the attestation.

questions.hop_count_basis: Three necessary steps, the third crossing enactments. First, the rules that govern the witnesses at the moment of execution: rule (8) on their number and the form of their subscription and rule (12) on the presence in which everyone signs, both owed as duties under the chapeau of section 31. Second, the rule (9) vetting and declaration step, which controls whom the notary may accept before those signatures are taken and whose October 2018 wording has to be recovered from the amending Acts. Third, the step out of the Notaries Ordinance into section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, which disqualifies a beneficiary from attesting; nothing in section 31 says this, so it cannot be reached without the second enactment. Rule (20)(a) and (c) are counted within the earlier steps rather than as a fourth, because they only require the notary to record facts the other rules already oblige him to secure. The supporting provisions add no further necessary link.

enrichment.original_background: The Notary knows the testator who wishes to execute a last Will and who is sick and taking treatment warded in a hospital. He is of the opinion that the testator is of sound mind memory and understanding.
enrichment.enriched_background: The Notary knows the testator who wishes to execute a last Will and who is sick and taking treatment warded in a hospital. He is of the opinion that the testator is of sound mind memory and understanding. The testator is Wijesuriya Arachchige Piyasena, aged 74, a retired schoolteacher of No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, who has been warded since 3 October 2018 in Ward 7 of the general hospital at Kandy for treatment of a heart condition. The Notary is Sujeewa Bandara, who is authorised to practise in Sinhala in the judicial zone in which the hospital stands. The Will is written in Sinhala on two sheets and is to be signed at the testator's bedside on 12 October 2018; the testator is literate in Sinhala, can read the Will for himself and can sign his name in letters. By the Will the testator devises his house and land at No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, being Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 3312, to his daughter; bequeaths one undivided half share of a coconut land at Alawatugoda to his nephew Ranjith Kumara; and leaves Rs. 500,000 from his savings account to a neighbour. The two people first offered to the Notary to sign as witnesses are that nephew, Ranjith Kumara, who has come to the ward for the purpose, and Kumudini Silva, a nurse on duty who first met the testator when he was admitted four days earlier and who does not know his occupation or where he lives. Also willing to come to the ward are two neighbours, H. M. Gunapala, a retired postmaster of No. 40, Temple Road, and D. A. Nandawathie of No. 46, Temple Road; each has known the testator for more than twenty years, knows his proper name, his occupation and his residence, takes nothing under the Will, is literate in Sinhala and can sign in letters, and neither is married to anyone who takes under the Will. The hospital raises no objection to the Notary and both witnesses remaining together at the bedside for as long as the signing takes.

added_facts.fact: The testator is Wijesuriya Arachchige Piyasena, aged 74, a retired schoolteacher of No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, warded since 3 October 2018 in Ward 7 of the general hospital at Kandy; the Notary is Sujeewa Bandara, authorised to practise in Sinhala in the judicial zone in which the hospital stands.

added_facts.fact: The Will is written in Sinhala on two sheets and is to be signed at the testator's bedside on 12 October 2018; the testator is literate in Sinhala, can read the Will himself and can sign his name in letters.
added_facts.reason: The original background says only that a last Will is to be executed. Rule (11) is engaged only where the executant cannot read the instrument or asks for it to be read, and rule (20)(d) requires the attestation to say which course was taken, so the testator's literacy and the date and place of signing have to be settled.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the testator could not read the Will, the Notary would have to read and explain it to him, though even then rule (11) would not require that to be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses, because wills and codicils are excepted.

added_facts.fact: By the Will the testator devises his house and land at No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, being Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 3312, to his daughter, bequeaths one undivided half share of a coconut land at Alawatugoda to his nephew Ranjith Kumara, and leaves Rs. 500,000 from his savings account to a neighbour.

added_facts.reason: Makes the witness question determinate. One proposed witness is a beneficiary, which engages section 11; the other is a stranger to the testator's circumstances, which is the situation rule (9) addresses and which would leave the Notary unable to complete from the witnesses' own knowledge the particulars rule (20)(c) requires.

Rule (8) requires two witnesses who subscribe their signatures in letters and rule (9) requires persons of good repute well acquainted with the executant.

added_facts.fact: The hospital raises no objection to the Notary and both witnesses remaining together at the testator's bedside for as long as the signing takes.
added_facts.reason: Rule (12) requires the testator and both witnesses to sign in the Notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and rule (24) requires the same signatures on the protocol. Whether the ward permits all of them to stay together decides whether that can be done at one sitting.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a witness had to leave the ward before the testator and the other witness had signed, the Notary could not lawfully attest, and attesting in that state of affairs would expose him to the offence in section 39(c).

gold_answer_draft.issue: What precautions must the Notary take with regard to the witnesses when the testator, who is warded in hospital, executes his last Will: how many witnesses are needed, whom he may accept and whom he must refuse, in whose presence the Will and the protocol must be signed, and what he must obtain from the witnesses and state about them in his attestation.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance makes each of its rules a duty of the notary. Rule (8) forbids him to attest any instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters. Rule (9), in the form it bore in October 2018, allowed him to proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had first to satisfy himself that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their declaration to that effect signed at the foot of the instrument. Rule (12) requires the executant and the witnesses to sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another and the notary to sign in the presence of them all; attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time of execution is an offence under Notaries Ordinance s.39(c). Rule (13) forbids him to attest an instrument to which he is himself a party. Rule (11) obliges him to read over and explain the instrument where the executant cannot read it or asks for it to be read, but expressly excepts wills and codicils from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses. Rule (20) requires the attestation to state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another (paragraph (a)), the date and place of execution and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences (paragraph (c)), and whether the instrument was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses (paragraph (d)). Rule (24) requires the protocol copy to carry the signatures of the party and the witnesses to the original. Outside the Notaries Ordinance, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 makes a beneficial gift utterly null and void so far as concerns an attesting witness, that witness's spouse and anyone claiming under them, though by s.10 the will is not invalidated by an attesting witness's incompetency, and by s.12 and s.13 a charged creditor or a named executor is not disqualified. Section 7 of the same Ordinance requires any alteration made after execution to be executed in the same manner as the will.
gold_answer_draft.application: Two witnesses are needed and each must sign in letters. Of the two people first offered at the ward, the nephew Ranjith Kumara takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will; if he attests it, that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11), so the Notary must not accept him. The nurse Kumudini Silva met the testator only on his admission four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence. The Notary's own knowledge of the testator satisfies the identification limb of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, so the Will is not exposed on that ground, but she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that the rule contemplates and cannot speak to the particulars the Notary must record under rule (20)(c), so she should not be accepted either. The two neighbours, Gunapala and Nandawathie, meet the conditions: they are two, they are literate in Sinhala and can subscribe in letters as rule (8) requires, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take under the Will. Since the ward allows all of them to remain at the bedside, the Notary should have the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and then sign himself in front of them, as rules (12) and (24) require, which also keeps him clear of s.39(c). He should take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will. Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, rule (11) requires no reading over, and wills are in any event excepted from reading over in the witnesses' presence, but under rule (20)(d) the attestation must record which course was taken, and under rule (20)(a) and (c) it must state that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and give the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of both neighbours. If anything in the Will has to be altered after signing, s.7 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requires the alteration to be executed in the same manner, so the witnesses are needed again.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Notary should use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; choose witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, which the nurse is not and the two neighbours are; satisfy himself that each witness can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' signed declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and set out in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses. This list is drawn from the provisions recorded in this map. Rule (10) of Notaries Ordinance s.31, which was in force in October 2018 and was repealed in 2024, is not reproduced in the corpus, so the possibility of a further witness-related requirement in that rule cannot be excluded from the corpus text.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance imposes on every notary a duty strictly to observe the rules set out in that section, so the requirements about witnesses are duties and not matters of practice.
A notary may not attest a will unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures to it in letters, so there must be two witnesses and each must sign his name rather than make a mark.

Under rule (9) as it stood at the matter date the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the person executing the instrument or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had to satisfy himself before accepting them that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
The testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in the presence of the testator and of the attesting witnesses.
Attesting a deed without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is an offence under section 39 of the Notaries Ordinance.

The attestation must state that the instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and must give the place of execution and the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses.

Where a will gives a beneficial interest to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance makes the gift utterly null and void so far as concerns the attesting witness, the spouse and anyone claiming under them, although by section 10 the will itself is not invalidated by the incompetency of an attesting witness.
The notary himself may not be a party to the instrument he attests, so he cannot make up the two witnesses by signing as one of them.
The witnesses to the original will must also sign the protocol copy that the notary preserves.

Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but for wills and codicils this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and the attestation must record which course was followed.
Any alteration made to the will after execution has no effect unless it is executed in the same manner as the will itself, which requires the witnesses again.

The nephew who takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will must not be accepted as an attesting witness, because if he attests the Will that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned.

The nurse who met the testator four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence is not a witness the Notary can safely accept, because she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that rule (9) contemplates and cannot supply from her own knowledge the particulars of the testator that the attestation must carry; the Notary's own knowledge of the testator meets the identification limb of rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, but it does not cure her inability to speak to those matters.

The two neighbours are suitable witnesses: there are two of them, each is literate in Sinhala and can subscribe his signature in letters, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take anything under the Will.

Because the ward allows the Notary and both witnesses to remain at the bedside throughout, the Notary can secure that the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and that he then signs in front of all of them, which also protects him from the offence of attesting without the attesting witnesses appearing personally before him.

Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, the Notary need only record in his attestation that it was read over by the testator, and he must in any event enter in the attestation the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of the two neighbours.

The precautions the Notary should take about witnesses are therefore: use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; use witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and so refuse the nurse and use the two neighbours instead; satisfy himself that each can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and record in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses.

questions.block_reason: Two matters need a lawyer before this can stand as gold. First, the ground on which the answer refuses the nurse as a witness is disputed: on the October 2018 wording of rule (9), recovered only from Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) and Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), the vetting and declaration duty attached where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator himself; rule (20)(c) requires the witnesses' own full names and residences, not their knowledge of the testator's particulars, so it does not carry the weight the answer puts on it. Second, completeness cannot be established from the corpus: rule (10) of section 31 was in force in October 2018 and was repealed only by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(4) without being reproduced, and the pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b), the witness-facing attestation paragraph, is likewise not recoverable, so a question asking for the precautions relating to witnesses cannot be answered exhaustively from the corpus text.
